chunks: From him, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he said:

Regarding a man who swore an oath not to speak to a relative of his, he said: 'It is not binding, so let him speak to the one he swore not to speak to.' And he said: 'Every oath not intended for the sake of Allah is not binding, whether in divorce or otherwise.'

Al-Halabi said: 'And I asked him about a woman who designated her wealth as a sacrifice (hady) for the House of Allah, if she lent her belongings to so-and-so and so-and-so, and some of her family lent them without her permission.' He said: 'There is no sacrifice upon her. The sacrifice is only that which is designated for Allah as a sacrifice for the Kaaba; that is what is fulfilled when designated for Allah. And what is similar to this is not binding, and there is no sacrifice except with the mention of Allah.'
And he was asked about a man who says: 'Upon me is a thousand camels,' while he is in the state of ihram for a thousand pilgrimages. He said: 'That is from the steps of Satan.'
And regarding a man who says: 'He is in ihram for a pilgrimage,' he said: 'It is not binding.' Or he says: 'I am sacrificing this food,' he said: 'It is not binding, for food is not sacrificed.'

Or he says: 'The carcass, after it has been slaughtered, he is sacrificing it to the House of Allah, Exalted.' He said: 'Only the young camels are sacrificed while they are alive, and they are not sacrificed when they become meat.'

key_terms.بَدَنَة: A young camel used for sacrifice
key_terms.خُطَوَاتُ الشَّيْطَانِ: Steps of Satan (minor or insignificant acts)
key_terms.مُحْرِم: One in the state of ihram (pilgrimal consecration)

ai.seo_question: What are the conditions for a vow to be binding and what constitutes a valid sacrifice (hady) in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the jurisprudential nuances of vows (nadhr) and sacrifices (hady), emphasizing that validity hinges on the intention of dedicating the act specifically to Allah rather than mere verbal declaration. It establishes that casual vows or those not explicitly intended for the Kaaba are not binding, and specifies that valid sacrifices must be living animals designated for the Kaaba, excluding food or slaughtered carcasses. This reflects the Shia scholarly emphasis on the precision of intention (niyyah) and the specific conditions of the object of sacrifice in ritual purity and obligation.
